title: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk
hook: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukkha, the wobble in the wheel. Your line was this too. Did something small go wrong, and did the words help? Day four.

Picture a prince in the foothills of the Himalayas, around two and a half thousand years ago. His father has given him everything. Palaces, music, fine clothes, and, the story says, a life kept carefully away from anything ugly. Then one day he goes out riding. By the road he sees an old man, bent over. Then a sick man. Then a dead body being carried to the fire. Then a wandering monk, owning nothing, and somehow calm. Four sights. He goes home and can't stop thinking about them. That rich kid is the person the whole path is named after.
screen: `A PRINCE WHO HAD EVERYTHING.` → `FOUR SIGHTS BY THE ROAD.` → `HE CAN'T STOP THINKING.`

segments.voice: Buddha isn't a name. It's a title. It comes from a Pali and Sanskrit root, budh, to wake up. A buddha is someone who has woken up. His name was Siddhattha, of the Gotama family, from the Sakya people, in the borderlands of what's now Nepal and India. Historians place him somewhere in the fifth or sixth century before the common era; the exact dates are argued about. The four sights you just heard are how later tellings of his life begin, and that's worth being honest about. The oldest discourses tell a very similar story about an earlier buddha, and the Buddha himself remembers his young life more plainly: a comfortable home, and a growing shock at aging, sickness and death. The four sights may be a story. The question inside them is real. Here's what that rich kid did with it. He left the palace, lived for years as a wandering seeker, nearly starved himself, gave that up, sat down under a tree, and woke up. Then he spent about forty-five years walking the roads of northern India, teaching anyone who would listen: kings, farmers, beggars, women, people from every caste. And here's the part that surprises people. In the oldest texts he never claims to be a god. When someone asks what he is, a god or a spirit or a man, the story goes that he answers simply: awake. Theravada Buddhists especially emphasize that he was a human being who found a way and showed it. Many Mahayana traditions also speak of the Buddha on a vaster, cosmic scale. But in every school, the story starts with a person.
screen: `BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP.` · `SIDDHATTHA GOTAMA, OF THE SAKYAS.` · `THE PALACE, THE ROAD, THE TREE.` · `NOT A GOD. AWAKE.` · then, large: `HE WAS A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of an old face you know. On the second, think of someone who is sick, or has been. On the third, think of the calmest person you've ever met. The same four sights he saw are all around you, all the time. For three breaths, let yourself see them, the way he did.
The Buddha. Not a name but a title: the one who woke up. A person who found a way, and spent his life showing it. Fourth word.
Your line: he was a person. Today, look at one statue, picture or image of the Buddha you pass, on a shelf, in a shop, online, and remember: a real human being started this. Day four.

howItsDone: Buddhists honor the Buddha as a teacher and example, bowing to his image, offering flowers, light and incense at shrines, and celebrating his birth, awakening and death, often together on the festival of Vesak.

fork.setup: someone meets the Buddha on the road and asks: are you a god? a spirit? a man? what does he answer, in the story?
fork.reveal: he answers that he is awake: a buddha. not a claim to godhood, and not quite 'just a man' either. a person who woke up.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakened, from the root budh, to wake up.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha is the god of Buddhism.
what it means: a title, the awakened one, for a man named Siddhattha Gotama who found a way and taught it for about forty-five years.
what a scholar hears: buddha, past participle of budh. the four-sights story comes from later biographies; in the Digha Nikaya (DN 14) a similar story is told of an earlier buddha, Vipassi.

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the four sights told of the earlier buddha Vipassi
Sukhamala Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.38): his own memory of a sheltered youth

notes: Dates: stated as 'the fifth or sixth century BCE; the exact dates are argued about.' Confirm framing.
Four sights: presented as coming from later tellings (e.g., the Nidanakatha); the canon's DN 14 tells it of Vipassi. Confirm.
The Dona Sutta (AN 4.36) exchange (god, gandhabba, yakkha, human? — 'remember me as awake') is paraphrased and simplified to 'a god or a spirit or a man'. Confirm.
Theravada/Mahayana framing of the Buddha's nature: confirm this is fair to both.
'About forty-five years' of teaching is the traditional figure. Confirm.
